newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels could quickly asphyxiate Zaire capital.
newsitem.headline: Rebels could quickly asphyxiate Zaire capital.

text.p: Conditions in Kinshasa could deteriorate rapidly if vital supply routes are cut by rebels threatening to advance on the sprawling Zairean capital to dislodge President Mobutu Sese Seko, traders and bankers say.

For several months importers have allowed stocks of food and other products to dwindle for fear of a round of looting by Zaire's poorly paid and ill-disciplined army, business and public sector sources say.
Retail traders, notably Lebanese, say existing stocks are kept in secure warehouses far from outlets for fear of looting by defeated government soldiers.
Kinshasa relies on the port of Matadi, 300 km (180 miles) away at the mouth of the vast Zaire River, for most of its imported food, medicines, petrol, and other vital commodities.

Matadi links Kinshasa to the Atlantic Ocean via road and rail. A petrol pipeline and electricity pylons leading from the Inga hydroelectric dam feed the capital with its energy needs from the Western region known as Bas Zaire (Lower Zaire).
"Normally businesses maintain around three months worth of stocks. But since December they have reduced supplies for fear of looting," a prominent Kinshasa businessman told Reuters.
"If Kinshasa is cut off from the West, serious food shortages could be felt within three weeks," he added.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila says his forces will be in Kinshasa in three weeks. He claimed in a rally in Zaire's second city Lubumbashi on Saturday that he had already recruited 100,000 youths from Lower Zaire for the new offensive.

Diplomats and military analysts place his forces within 500 km (300 miles) of Kinshasa, and say he is building up troops and weaponry in the city of Kananga 600 km (370 miles) away in preparation for an advance from the east.

Forces from the elite presidential guard are preparing to resist the advance, but even if they succeed the threat of a siege may be enough to force the surrender of the collapsing army in its last stronghold, analysts say.

After weeks of persistent rumours that rebels are building up forces in the neighbouring Angolan province of Cabinda, fears are rife that Kabila could begin the siege by cutting off Kinshasa's supplies from the West.
Some shipping companies are already reluctant to dock at Matadi for fear the war may soon reach the port.

At least one businessman has already started an alternative route importing food and other supplies via the Congolese port of Pointe-Noire, and transporting by train to Brazzaville and barge accross the Zaire River to Kinshasa.
Prices would skyrocket beyond the reach of the desperately impoverished inhabitants, businessmen and diplomats say, if this route became the only one available.
According to sources in the petroleum sector fuel in Kinshasa could run out within one month if rebels cut the pipeline from Matadi.

The 300-km (180-mile) pipeline holds over a month's supplies, but if rebels cut it close to the capital, the sources say, stocks already on site would run out in under a month at normal consumption levels.
It would take up to six weeks for the beer taps to run dry in Kinshasa's breweries if imported malt and rice were blocked, brewery sources say.
Electricity is perhaps the least likely fuse the rebels may wish to blow. The Inga dam supplies not only Kinshasa, but most of Zaire as well as neighbouring states like Zambia and Congo.
"If they cut off the current they cut not only Kinshasa but most of the rest of Zaire which they control. It would bring all their new mining activities to a halt," a prominent banker said.
